analysis.one_liner: Gives Supreme Court justices 18-year terms, with a new seat opening every two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to give Supreme Court justices 18-year terms never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end lifetime active service on the Supreme Court. Each justice would serve 18 years in regular active service, with one new seat opening in the first and third years after each presidential election. The longest-serving sitting justices would step off the Court in seniority order as new justices are appointed, and recently retired justices would fill any gaps so the Court always has nine members.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a Supreme Court whose membership turns over on a predictable schedule instead of depending on justices' lifespans. Regularized, staggered appointments would lower the stakes of any single vacancy, reducing the incentive for political warfare over each seat and giving every president an equal, limited number of appointments. The reform would also keep any one justice's ideological leanings locked onto the Court for three or four decades.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting a less entrenched Court

how_it_helps.text: Sets an 18-year term of regular active service for each Supreme Court justice, after which the justice is deemed retired from active service.

Requires the President to nominate and the Senate to confirm one justice in the first and third years after each presidential election, creating a regular vacancy roughly every two years and ending the lottery over when seats open.

Phases out sitting justices in order of seniority — the longest-serving current justice would retire as each new justice is commissioned — rather than letting lifetime tenure keep any one seat frozen for decades.

Keeps the Court at full strength by directing the most recently retired justice to serve temporarily whenever a vacancy, disability, or disqualification drops the membership below the number set by law.

analysis.who_pays: The sitting justices with the longest tenure lose the most: they would be pushed into senior status on a fixed schedule, giving up lifetime seats on the active Court. Presidents and senators would lose the outsized payoff of an unpredictable vacancy, since appointments would no longer hinge on when a justice happens to die or retire.

drawbacks.text: The bill would force out all nine sitting justices on a rolling schedule, not just future ones — critics would call that a partisan restructuring of a Court whose current majority the sponsoring party opposes.

The Constitution says federal judges hold their offices 'during good Behaviour,' and although the bill tries to work around this by having justices keep their office in senior status after 18 years, legal scholars dispute whether Congress can impose term limits on Supreme Court justices by statute rather than by constitutional amendment.

The fixed formula of one appointment in the first and third years after each presidential election guarantees every president two seats per term regardless of need, and bars any appointment outside that schedule even in unusual circumstances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reform tackles a real problem — individual justices now shaping national law for 30 to 40 years, with each vacancy becoming a national political crisis — and the staggered 18-year design is the most widely discussed version of the fix. But the bill applies the change to sitting justices rather than prospectively, which raises both constitutional doubts and guaranteed partisan resistance, and its bare-bones 8-cosponsor support suggests its sponsors knew it had no realistic path in this Congress. A more politically durable version would grandfather current justices.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on July 26, 2022, joined by six original cosponsors including Judiciary Chairman Jerrold Nadler.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which took no further action on it for three months.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — the customary holding step for a bill leadership does not intend to move.
The bill ended with 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nine sitting Supreme Court justices keep their lifetime active seats, and the political parties keep the enormous, unpredictable payoff of fighting over whatever vacancy a justice's death or retirement happens to create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting justices and party vacancy battles

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and all 8 cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so no opposition votes were ever recorded, and no Republican is listed as a supporter.

industries.note: The bill ends their most valuable asset: a lifetime seat on the nation's highest court. The three longest-serving justices would have been the first forced off as new appointments arrived, so the bill's fate rested entirely with the political class, not with any popular constituency.

Regularizing two appointments per presidential term would remove the jackpot of unpredictable vacancies that parties currently fight over, but it would also guarantee each president two seats per term and take away the extra appointments a lucky president can now win. Their stake in preserving the existing vacancy lottery is one reason reforms like this rarely advance.
